title: Solar PV Systems: Design and Installation Basics
summary: Learn how solar panels work, audit a home's energy needs, size panels, batteries and inverters, and install, maintain and cost a system safely, with worked calculations.
audience: Electricians, technicians, students, homeowners and small-business owners

body.p: A solar photovoltaic (PV) panel turns sunlight directly into electricity. Each panel is made of many cells of silicon. When light falls on a cell, it knocks electrons loose and a built-in electric field pushes them in one direction, so the cell produces direct current (DC). Cells are wired together into a panel, and panels into an array, to reach a useful voltage and power.

Panels are rated in watts peak (Wp): the power they give under standard test conditions of 1000 watts of sunlight per square metre at 25 °C. A 400 W panel with an area of 1.9 m² therefore converts about 400 / (1000 x 1.9), roughly 21%, of the sunlight into electricity. Real output is usually lower because of heat, dust, shading and the angle of the sun.

list: Monocrystalline panels: dark, higher efficiency, common today.
Polycrystalline panels: bluish, slightly less efficient, often cheaper.
Panel output falls as panels get hot, so leave an air gap behind them.
Shade on even part of a panel can cut the output of the whole string.
Panels make DC electricity in daylight.
A charge controller manages charging of the batteries.
Batteries store energy for the night and cloudy days.
An inverter converts DC to the alternating current (AC) used by most appliances.
Protection (fuses, breakers, earthing) and correctly sized cables keep it safe.

body.tip: A system with no batteries that feeds a building while the grid is on is called grid-tied. A system with batteries that works without the grid is called off-grid. A hybrid system can do both.

lessons.title: Working out how much energy you need

body.p: Sizing starts with a load audit: list every appliance, its power in watts and how many hours a day it runs. Energy in watt-hours (Wh) equals power multiplied by time. Getting this list right matters more than any other step, because every later choice depends on it.

list: 5 LED bulbs of 10 W for 5 hours: 5 x 10 x 5 = 250 Wh.
A TV of 80 W for 4 hours: 320 Wh.
A small fridge: about 1200 Wh a day (check the energy label; the compressor cycles on and off).
4 phones charged at 10 W for 2 hours: 80 Wh.
A laptop of 60 W for 4 hours: 240 Wh.

body.p: The total daily need is 250 + 320 + 1200 + 80 + 240 = 2090 Wh, or about 2.1 kWh a day. Notice that the fridge uses more than half. Cutting demand is the cheapest way to cut system cost: an efficient fridge or switching off devices on standby can save more money than buying extra panels.

Also note which appliances run at the same time. Here, if everything is on together, the running load is 50 + 80 + 150 + 60 + 40 = 380 W. Motors in fridges, pumps and power tools draw a surge of up to about three times their running power for a moment when they start. This affects the size of the inverter.

body.tip: Read the label on each appliance, or measure it with a plug-in energy meter. Guesses are usually too low.

body.p: Peak sun hours (PSH) express a day's sunlight as the number of hours of full 1000 W/m² sun. Much of Africa receives about 4.5 to 6 peak sun hours a day, but the figure changes by place and season, so use local data for the worst month you need to cover.

Array size (W) = daily energy (Wh) / (peak sun hours x system efficiency). The efficiency, often taken as about 0.75, allows for heat, dust, wiring and battery losses. For the 2090 Wh load with 5 peak sun hours: 2090 / (5 x 0.75) is about 557 W. Two 300 W panels (600 W) would cover it with a small margin.
Check the other way round too: 600 W x 5 h x 0.75 = 2250 Wh a day, a little more than the 2090 Wh needed.

list: South of the equator, face panels north; north of the equator, face them south.
Tilt them at roughly the local latitude, with at least about 10 degrees so rain washes off dust.
Avoid shade from trees, walls and water tanks at all times of day.
Mount them securely against wind, with an air gap for cooling.

body.tip: Plan for growth. It is cheaper to choose a controller and inverter with room for an extra panel than to replace them later.

body.p: Batteries store daytime energy for use at night. Their capacity is given in amp-hours (Ah) at a voltage; energy (Wh) = Ah x V. A 24 V 120 Ah battery bank stores 24 x 120 = 2880 Wh.

You should not empty a battery fully. The usable share is the depth of discharge (DoD): about 80% or more for lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) batteries and about 50% for lead-acid batteries if they are to last. Required capacity = daily energy x days of autonomy / DoD.

list: For one day of 2090 Wh with lithium (DoD 0.8): 2090 / 0.8 = 2612.5 Wh. At 24 V that is about 109 Ah, so a 24 V 120 Ah bank gives 2880 x 0.8 = 2304 Wh usable, enough.
For two days with lead-acid (DoD 0.5) at 12 V: 2 x 2090 / 0.5 / 12 is about 697 Ah, a heavy and expensive bank.
Lithium costs more at first but lasts many more cycles and needs no topping up.
Use batteries of the same type, age and capacity in a bank.
Fit a fuse or breaker close to the battery positive terminal.
Keep batteries ventilated, cool and out of children's reach.
Use a battery management system (BMS) with lithium batteries.

body.tip: Higher system voltages (24 V or 48 V) mean lower currents for the same power, so thinner cables and smaller losses.

body.p: The charge controller sits between panels and batteries and stops overcharging. PWM controllers are simple and cheap; MPPT controllers adjust the panel voltage to harvest more power, often 10 to 30% more, especially in cool weather or when panel voltage is much higher than battery voltage.

The inverter must handle the running load with a margin and the starting surge. For the example home, the running load is 380 W. With a 25% margin the continuous rating should be at least 1.25 x 380 = 475 W. If the 150 W fridge surges to three times its running power at start, the peak is about 380 - 150 + 450 = 680 W, so choose an inverter whose surge rating exceeds that. A pure sine-wave inverter is safest for electronics and motors.

list: Cables must be thick enough for the current; undersized cables heat up and waste energy.
Keep battery-to-inverter cables short.
Use DC-rated breakers and isolators on the panel and battery side.
Losses multiply: a 90% efficient inverter and a 97% efficient controller turn 10 kWh into about 10 x 0.9 x 0.97 = 8.73 kWh.

body.tip: Follow the manufacturer's manuals and local wiring regulations, and have mains connections made by a qualified electrician.

body.p: Solar systems are low-maintenance but not no-maintenance. Panels produce voltage whenever light falls on them, so DC parts can be live even when the inverter is switched off. Work at height needs proper ladders and harnesses. Batteries can deliver very large currents, so cover terminals and remove rings and watches.

list: Clean panels with water and a soft brush when dusty, early or late in the day.
Check for shading from new growth or buildings.
Inspect cables and connectors for damage and tightness.
Check battery state of charge and controller logs or app data.
Keep a maintenance record with dates and readings.

body.p: Simple payback = system cost / annual savings. A system costing R45 000 that saves R600 a month on electricity or generator fuel pays back in 45 000 / 600 = 75 months, or 6.25 years. Panels often last 25 years, but batteries may need replacing after about 5 to 15 years, so include that in your sums. Reliability during power cuts also has value that the payback figure leaves out.

body.tip: Get at least two quotes, ask for the load calculation and component data sheets, and check that the installer is accredited where a scheme exists.
